questions.question: A stable patient is secured to a wheeled stretcher on a clear, level route to the ambulance. Which movement plan is most appropriate?

choices.text: Roll the stretcher along the route
Carry the stretcher with four providers along the entire route
Transfer the patient to a backboard solely to carry the same route
Use a stair chair to replace the stretcher despite the absence of stairs

questions.explanation: Rolling is preferred when the situation permits because it reduces the need for carrying.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Four providers can improve carrying safety, but unnecessary carrying adds lifting demands.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: A backboard is not needed merely to replace available rolling transport.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: The scenario provides no stair or seated-transport need.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: Four providers can make a necessary carry safer.
questions.whyNotBest: Four providers can improve carrying safety, but unnecessary carrying adds lifting demands.
questions.keyDistinction: Rolling is preferred when the situation permits because it reduces the need for carrying.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: The Wheeled Ambulance Stretcher · Rolling versus carrying

questions.question: Four providers are ready to lift, but they disagree about when to start and where to stand. What should happen before the lift?

choices.text: The leader assigns positions, describes the sequence, and uses a coordinated command
Each provider chooses a comfortable position and lifts when ready
The strongest provider begins lifting so the others can follow
The team discusses the sequence after the stretcher is raised

questions.explanation: A coordinated lift requires assigned positions, a shared sequence, and preparatory commands.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Individual readiness does not provide synchronized movement.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Following an unannounced lift can produce uneven loading.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Planning after lifting is too late.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: Each provider does need a safe position and readiness.
questions.whyNotBest: Individual readiness does not provide synchronized movement.
questions.keyDistinction: A coordinated lift requires assigned positions, a shared sequence, and preparatory commands.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Directions and Commands · Coordinated team movement

questions.question: Which adjustment most directly reduces leverage and strain on an EMT’s back during a lift?

choices.text: Keeping the load close to the body while lifting
Holding the load farther forward to improve visibility
Reaching across the patient without changing foot position
Turning the upper body while keeping the feet planted

questions.explanation: Keeping the load close reduces leverage on the back; use an upright posture, the legs, and coordinated movement.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Holding the load farther away increases the strain.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Overreaching increases strain; repositioning is preferable.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Twisting under load is a lifting hazard.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Body Mechanics · Load distance and lifting strain

questions.question: Which sequence uses the power lift to raise a patient-carrying device?

choices.text: Balance the feet → bend the legs with back upright → grasp close to the body → extend the legs
Balance the feet → bend the waist with knees straight → grasp → extend the back
Lock the knees → reach forward with extended arms → raise with the shoulders
Bend the legs → grasp → twist the torso while rising

questions.explanation: The power lift uses properly placed flexed legs to raise the load while maintaining upright alignment and keeping it close.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Bending and extending the back transfers lifting demands to the back.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Straight knees and forward reaching do not use the leg-powered technique.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Twisting introduces lateral force during the lift.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Body Mechanics · Power lift

questions.question: An EMT says, “My back stayed straight,” but lifted while bent far forward at the hips. What is the best assessment of the technique?

choices.text: It can still strain the back because the torso was not upright over the pelvis
It is safe because straightness alone prevents strain regardless of torso angle
It is safer than a leg-powered lift because the hips provide all the lifting force
It is safe if the hands are held farther from the legs

questions.explanation: Keeping the back straight does not make lifting safe when the torso is significantly bent forward at the hips.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Straightness alone does not maintain the upright load alignment.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: A leg-powered lift with proper alignment is the preferred method.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Holding the load farther away adds strain.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: A straight back is an important part of proper mechanics.
questions.whyNotBest: Straightness alone does not maintain the upright load alignment.
questions.keyDistinction: Keeping the back straight does not make lifting safe when the torso is significantly bent forward at the hips.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Body Mechanics · Straight versus upright back

questions.question: Which hand position correctly describes a power grip on a stretcher handle?

choices.text: Palms up, fingers curled firmly, with the handle supported on the curved palms
Palms down, with the handle supported mainly by the fingertips
Palms up, with fingers spread and the handle hanging from the fingertips
Palms facing each other, with the handle resting across the thumbs alone

questions.explanation: A power grip fully supports the handle in the curved palms with a firm finger grip.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: The palms should face up and support the handle.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Fingertip support and spread fingers weaken the grip.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Thumb-only support is not the power grip.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Body Mechanics · Power grip

questions.question: A supine patient needs transfer from a bed to a nearby stretcher. Two rescuers plan a draw sheet move. Which approach fits this method?

choices.text: Use the sheet or blanket beneath the patient to support the coordinated transfer
Pull the patient’s shirt while the second rescuer pushes the legs
One rescuer pulls both wrists while the other holds the bed stationary
Use a direct carry but leave the sheet on the bed

questions.explanation: A draw sheet transfer uses the sheet or blanket beneath the patient with two or more rescuers.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Clothing traction is not the draw sheet method.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Wrist traction is not a sheet-supported transfer.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: A direct carry is a different technique.

sourceReferences.locator: XI.D.2. Draw sheet method; VI.C. Bed drag

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: Both plans involve two rescuers, but the support used matters.
questions.whyNotBest: Clothing traction is not the draw sheet method.
questions.keyDistinction: A draw sheet transfer uses the sheet or blanket beneath the patient with two or more rescuers.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Nonurgent Moves · Draw sheet transfer

questions.question: An EMT cannot complete a bed transfer without reaching far across the mattress. What adjustment best follows safe reaching principles?

choices.text: Kneel on the bed, pull in controlled increments, and reposition rather than overreach
Keep both feet on the floor and extend the arms farther on each pull
Bend farther at the waist so the hands can reach the opposite edge
Pull continuously without repositioning until the patient reaches the edge

questions.explanation: Kneeling on the bed limits reaching distance; incremental pulling and repositioning maintain safer mechanics.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Increasing reach adds leverage and strain.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Bending farther does not correct excessive reach.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Continuous pulling without repositioning can force overreaching.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Principles of Safe Reaching and Pulling · Safe reaching

questions.question: Two EMTs are preparing to lift a stable patient estimated at 280 lb. Their stretcher can support the patient. What additional requirement remains?

choices.text: Arrange at least four providers for the lift
Proceed with two because the equipment capacity is sufficient
Attempt one lift with two before deciding whether assistance is needed
Use a power grip to substitute for additional providers

questions.explanation: The provided lifting guidance calls for at least four providers for a patient over 250 lb; equipment capacity and personnel capacity are separate concerns.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Equipment capacity does not establish that two providers can lift safely.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Assistance should be arranged before an unsafe trial.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: A good grip does not replace adequate lifting personnel.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyNotBest: Equipment capacity does not establish that two providers can lift safely.
questions.keyDistinction: The provided lifting guidance calls for at least four providers for a patient over 250 lb; equipment capacity and personnel capacity are separate concerns.

reviewReferences.section: Principles of Safe Lifting and Carrying · Weight and lifting resources

questions.question: A conscious, stable patient can safely sit upright and needs to descend a narrow flight of stairs. Which device best fits?

choices.text: Stair chair
Wheeled ambulance stretcher
Long backboard
Scoop stretcher

questions.explanation: A stair chair is suited to a conscious patient whose condition permits sitting during stair movement.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: A wheeled stretcher is less suited to a narrow stairway with a stable patient who can safely sit.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: A backboard is not the preferred seated stair-carry device for this patient.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: A scoop is intended for lifting a supine patient rather than seated stair transport.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: A wheeled stretcher is the common transport device on level ground.
questions.whyNotBest: A wheeled stretcher is less suited to a narrow stairway with a stable patient who can safely sit.
questions.keyDistinction: A stair chair is suited to a conscious patient whose condition permits sitting during stair movement.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Principles of Safe Lifting and Carrying · Stair chair selection

questions.question: During a stair-chair carry of a stable patient, one provider develops sudden sharp back pain. What is the best response?

choices.text: Coordinate a safe stop and obtain additional lifting assistance
Change grip and continue because stopping may delay transport
Switch to walking the patient without reassessing whether that is safe
Speed up the carry to shorten the time under load

questions.explanation: A provider who develops sharp pain should stop the move safely and request help rather than continue risking injury.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: A changed grip does not establish that continuing is safe.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: The patient’s ability to walk safely has not been established.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Rushing increases movement risk.

sourceReferences.locator: Question 2 · sudden sharp pain during stair-chair carry

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: A grip change can sometimes improve mechanics, but sudden sharp pain calls for stopping.
questions.whyNotBest: A changed grip does not establish that continuing is safe.
questions.keyDistinction: A provider who develops sharp pain should stop the move safely and request help rather than continue risking injury.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Personnel Considerations · Pain during stair movement

questions.question: Smoke and flames are advancing toward a trapped patient, and the crew cannot protect the patient at the current location. What takes priority?

choices.text: Move the patient to safety promptly while minimizing avoidable spinal movement
Complete the primary assessment and all indicated spinal packaging before moving
Wait for a full nonurgent lift plan despite the advancing hazard
Use the mechanism of injury alone to decide whether the hazard matters

questions.explanation: An immediate threat that cannot be controlled justifies an emergency move before assessment and care at the unsafe location.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Delaying for complete assessment and packaging prolongs exposure to the hazard.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Nonurgent planning does not fit advancing fire.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: The direct scene threat itself requires action.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: Assessment and spinal protection matter, but the scene threat changes the timing.
questions.whyNotBest: Delaying for complete assessment and packaging prolongs exposure to the hazard.
questions.keyDistinction: An immediate threat that cannot be controlled justifies an emergency move before assessment and care at the unsafe location.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Emergency Moves · Emergency move priority

questions.question: Immediate danger requires an EMT alone to remove an unresponsive patient from a vehicle. Which sequence best matches the one-person technique?

choices.text: Clear the legs from the pedals → turn the back toward the open door → support under the shoulders and head → drag to safety
Pull the torso out first → free the legs afterward → support the head once outside
Leave the feet at the pedals → pull both wrists through the door
Turn the chest toward the door → lift by the forearms without supporting the head

questions.explanation: The technique clears the legs first, turns the back toward the opening, and supports the patient through the armpits with the head against the rescuer’s body.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Pulling first risks leaving the legs caught and delays head support.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: The legs must be cleared and the described technique supports the upper body and head.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: The back faces the door, and head support remains important.

sourceReferences.locator: IX.D. Removing an unconscious patient from a vehicle while alone

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Emergency Moves · One-person emergency vehicle removal

questions.question: At a safe scene, a patient has shock and needs to be moved quickly. There is time for brief measures to limit spinal movement. Which category best fits?

choices.text: Urgent move
Emergency move solely because the patient has shock
Nonurgent move because there is no scene hazard
Routine transfer without regard to the patient’s condition

questions.explanation: Shock can require an urgent move; urgent movement allows brief consideration of spinal protection while proceeding quickly.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: An urgent care need at a safe scene is distinguished from movement forced by immediate danger.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: A safe scene does not make an unstable patient’s move nonurgent.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: The patient’s condition determines urgency.

sourceReferences.locator: X.A. Urgent Moves; chapter review of urgent moves

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: Both categories involve moving without unnecessary delay.
questions.whyNotBest: An urgent care need at a safe scene is distinguished from movement forced by immediate danger.
questions.keyDistinction: Shock can require an urgent move; urgent movement allows brief consideration of spinal protection while proceeding quickly.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Urgent Moves · Urgent versus emergency move

questions.question: Which patient has the strongest reason for rapid extrication from a vehicle?

choices.text: A patient who needs an immediate intervention that requires a supine position
A stable patient who can be fully assessed and treated in the current seat
A stable patient who prefers a faster departure despite no urgent care need
A patient selected solely because every collision requires rapid extrication

questions.explanation: An immediate intervention that cannot be performed seated provides a specific rapid-extrication indication.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Being able to assess and treat the stable patient in place does not establish urgency.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Preference for speed alone does not justify the additional risk.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Rapid extrication requires a specific indication rather than collision alone.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: Removal is eventually needed for transport, but not necessarily rapidly.
questions.whyNotBest: Being able to assess and treat the stable patient in place does not establish urgency.
questions.keyDistinction: An immediate intervention that cannot be performed seated provides a specific rapid-extrication indication.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Urgent Moves · Rapid extrication indications

questions.question: A stable patient is supine on the floor, has no suspected spinal injury, and must be carried a short distance to the stretcher. There is room for rescuers to stand side by side. Which method best fits?

choices.text: Direct ground lift
Extremity lift
Draw sheet transfer
Clothes drag

questions.explanation: A direct ground lift fits a supine patient without suspected spinal injury who needs carrying to the stretcher.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: The extremity lift is especially useful when confined space prevents side-by-side positioning.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: A draw sheet is suited to a bed-to-stretcher transfer.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: A clothes drag is an emergency movement technique; the stated scene allows a planned lift.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: An extremity lift can also be useful for some patients without suspected injury, especially in a small space.
questions.whyNotBest: The extremity lift is especially useful when confined space prevents side-by-side positioning.
questions.keyDistinction: A direct ground lift fits a supine patient without suspected spinal injury who needs carrying to the stretcher.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Nonurgent Moves · Nonurgent lift selection

questions.question: An older patient with marked spinal curvature cannot lie comfortably flat on a rigid board. Which consideration best guides packaging?

choices.text: Consider a device such as a vacuum mattress that can accommodate the patient’s shape
Explain the procedure compassionately but use the rigid flat surface without adapting support
Assume the discomfort is unrelated to packaging because the board is rigid
Use the same flat position regardless of skeletal rigidity or curvature

questions.explanation: Geriatric skeletal changes can make rigid supine packaging harmful; a vacuum mattress is an alternative that molds around the patient.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Reassurance helps, but does not resolve a surface that cannot safely accommodate the patient’s spinal curvature.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: The rigid surface may contribute to the problem.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Positioning should account for skeletal changes.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: A compassionate explanation helps reduce the patient’s fear.
questions.whyNotBest: Reassurance helps, but does not resolve a surface that cannot safely accommodate the patient’s spinal curvature.
questions.keyDistinction: Geriatric skeletal changes can make rigid supine packaging harmful; a vacuum mattress is an alternative that molds around the patient.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Geriatrics · Geriatric packaging

questions.question: What is bariatrics?

choices.text: The prevention or management of obesity and related diseases
The care of conditions associated with older age
The restriction of spinal movement after an injury
The assessment of breathing and gas exchange

questions.explanation: Bariatrics concerns obesity and associated diseases; geriatrics, spinal protection, and respiratory assessment concern other needs.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: This describes geriatrics.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: This describes spinal protection.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: This describes respiratory assessment.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded class material; not independently verified

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: XIII. Bariatrics

questions.question: A bariatric stretcher’s rated capacity exceeds the patient’s weight. What can the crew conclude from that fact alone?

choices.text: The rating supports equipment selection, but personnel, route, and lifting assistance still require evaluation
The rating guarantees that the usual two-person crew can manually lift the patient
A higher capacity eliminates the need to plan loading into the ambulance
Additional personnel are required only after the first lifting attempt fails

questions.explanation: Higher equipment capacity does not remove the danger to providers; safe movement still requires resource and route planning.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Equipment strength does not establish crew lifting ability.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Ambulance loading remains part of the move plan.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Help should be arranged before an unsafe attempt.

sourceReferences.locator: XIII.C. Higher-capacity equipment; XVII. Personnel Considerations

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: The rating is an essential equipment check.
questions.whyNotBest: Equipment strength does not establish crew lifting ability.
questions.keyDistinction: Higher equipment capacity does not remove the danger to providers; safe movement still requires resource and route planning.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Bariatrics · Equipment capacity versus provider safety

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches specialized equipment with its intended use?

choices.text: Basket stretcher: remote uneven terrain; flexible stretcher: confined spaces
Basket stretcher: routine seated stair carry; flexible stretcher: rigid spinal board
Scoop stretcher: use when only one side of the patient is accessible; stair chair: unresponsive supine transport
Flexible stretcher: rigid support for suspected spinal injury; basket stretcher: routine seated stair carry

questions.explanation: Basket stretchers serve remote or technical rescue settings; flexible stretchers conform around patients for confined-space movement.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Stair chairs serve suitable seated stair patients; flexible stretchers are not rigid boards.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: A scoop requires access to both sides; stair-chair use requires a conscious patient who can sit.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Flexible stretchers conform around the patient rather than providing rigid spinal support; the basket serves remote rescue rather than routine seated stair carry.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Additional Patient-Moving Equipment · Specialized stretcher selection

questions.question: After transporting a patient, a stretcher has no visible soil. What determines whether it is ready for the next patient?

choices.text: Completion of the required post-use decontamination process under local procedures
Visual appearance alone because no visible soil means no contamination
Secure storage alone because contamination ends once equipment is put away
Replacement of the mattress alone while leaving the frame and straps unaddressed

questions.explanation: Equipment must be decontaminated after use to protect patients and crews, following local procedures.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Invisible contamination is not excluded by appearance.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Storage does not replace decontamination.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: The process concerns equipment after use, not just one component.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: Inspection is useful, but visual cleanliness is not the whole requirement.
questions.whyNotBest: Invisible contamination is not excluded by appearance.
questions.keyDistinction: Equipment must be decontaminated after use to protect patients and crews, following local procedures.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Additional Patient-Moving Equipment · Decontamination between patients

questions.question: An unresponsive patient is breathing adequately and has no suspected spinal, hip, or pelvic injury. Which position best matches transport positioning guidance?

choices.text: Recovery position
Supine position
Fowler position
Prone position

questions.explanation: The recovery position is indicated for an unresponsive patient without the specified suspected injuries.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: An unresponsive patient breathing adequately without the stated injuries benefits from side positioning for airway drainage.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Fowler is generally used for a responsive patient who can maintain the position and benefits from sitting.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Prone is not the stated recovery-position guidance.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: Supine positioning is appropriate for some other conditions, including shock.
questions.whyNotBest: An unresponsive patient breathing adequately without the stated injuries benefits from side positioning for airway drainage.
questions.keyDistinction: The recovery position is indicated for an unresponsive patient without the specified suspected injuries.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Patient Positioning · Unresponsive patient positioning

questions.question: A conscious patient has nontraumatic chest discomfort and difficulty breathing, with no signs of shock. Which position is most appropriate?

choices.text: A position of comfort, usually Fowler or semi-Fowler
Supine with the legs elevated
Prone with the head turned to one side
Flat supine on a rigid backboard

questions.explanation: For a patient without suspected injury who has chest pain or respiratory distress, a comfortable upright or semi-upright position is typical.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Supine positioning may worsen breathing discomfort in this patient without shock.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Prone positioning does not provide the described relief of breathing difficulty.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: A rigid flat board is not indicated by this nontraumatic complaint.

questions.verificationStatus: Reviewed against uploaded course materials; not independently verified
questions.whyTempting: Supine positioning can be needed when circulation is compromised.
questions.whyNotBest: Supine positioning may worsen breathing discomfort in this patient without shock.
questions.keyDistinction: For a patient without suspected injury who has chest pain or respiratory distress, a comfortable upright or semi-upright position is typical.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 8 outline
reviewReferences.section: Patient Positioning · Chest discomfort and breathing

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches positioning to the patient’s needs?

choices.text: Suspected spinal injury: maintain required spinal restriction; nausea or vomiting: comfort with attention to airway protection
Suspected spinal injury: maintain required spinal restriction; nausea or vomiting: flat supine in every case for easier monitoring
Suspected spinal injury: freely adjust the torso for comfort; nausea or vomiting: comfort with attention to airway protection
Suspected spinal injury: freely adjust the torso for comfort; nausea or vomiting: flat supine in every case for easier monitoring

questions.explanation: Movement with suspected spinal injury must preserve appropriate restriction; positioning with vomiting must consider comfort and protect the airway.
